extracted.intended_audience: organizers and participants of AIM-focused mathematical workshops (research mathematicians, junior scientists, graduate students)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for planning, running, and participating in AIM-style focused research workshops in the mathematical sciences, emphasizing a specific mathematical goal, a fluid schedule, and collaborative afternoon working groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasis on a specific mathematical goal
rubrics_metrics.description: AIM focused workshops are distinguished by their emphasis on a specific mathematical goal, such as making progress on a significant unsolved problem, understanding the proof of an important new result, or examining the convergence of two distinct areas of mathematics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose a clear, specific goal for the workshop (progress on a problem, proof understanding, or area convergence) so activities are aligned and productive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Team-based, goal-oriented research forum
rubrics_metrics.description: AIM focused workshops provide an ideal forum for a team of researchers working together to map out strategies, set priorities, work toward a solution, and set in place a framework for progress on important mathematical problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure the workshop to support cooperative planning and sustained group effort; involve leaders in planning while ensuring junior scientists and graduate students are active participants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Morning schedule: two informal talks with long break
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two talks each day: both are in the morning, with a long break in between. The presentations are intended to be informal, with lots of questions and answers during the talks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan two morning talks focused on exposition and interaction rather than polished new-theorem announcements; schedule a long break between them and allow the lunch break to begin whenever the second talk ends (lunch is 2 hours).

rubrics_metrics.name: Talk content should be introductory and preparatory
rubrics_metrics.description: The talks tend to be introductory, serving as preparation for the afternoon activities; they usually are not about 'my latest big theorem.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Speakers should aim to introduce background, tools, and perspectives that enable collaborative afternoon work rather than presenting only cutting-edge, solitary results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Afternoon devoted to organized group activities (no talks)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are no talks in the afternoon. The afternoons are devoted to organized group activities. This could involve a large group discussion or breaking into smaller discussion groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design afternoon sessions around active engagement: discussions, problem lists, working on proofs or approaches, and 'ask the expert' sessions rather than passive listening.

rubrics_metrics.name: Small working groups of 4–6 participants
rubrics_metrics.description: The participants typically break into groups of 4 to 6 people to work on specific topics of interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form small groups focused on concrete tasks (understanding a proof, exploring approaches, starting sustained work) to maximize hands-on progress and interaction; ensure topics align with participants' interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Group topics: examples and repeatable topics
rubrics_metrics.description: Example topics include: understanding the details of a difficult proof or construction, discussing possible approaches to a problem, an 'ask the expert' session, or beginning work on a problem which will continue long after the workshop ends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage a variety of group topics, including both one-off sessions and sustained problem projects; allow some topics to repeat as needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Group reporting and cross‑communication
rubrics_metrics.description: Each group gives a brief report to the entire workshop at the beginning of the next afternoon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schedule short whole-group reports to share progress and cross-pollinate ideas; this keeps the larger group informed and can reconfigure activities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanism for selecting group topics to minimize overlap
rubrics_metrics.description: The AIM staff work with the organizers to determine an appropriate mechanism for selecting topics so that everyone has a group which interests them, but with a minimum of overlap so that people don't miss out on a topic of particular interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use organizer-prepared lists or collective group discussion to choose topics each day; aim for coverage and minimal conflict among popular topics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weekly schedule and social events
rubrics_metrics.description: Workshops run Monday–Friday, 9:00am to 5:00pm each day, with a 2-hour lunch break. Tuesday evening there is a reception and at 5:00 every day we have 'happy hour.' Workshop participants are welcome to arrive as early or stay as late as they wish. There are no afternoons off.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan formal hours and expect informal social interaction (reception, daily happy hour); set participant expectations about full-day engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fluid, on-site planning of schedule and speakers
rubrics_metrics.description: Only the first 5 or 6 talks are determined in advance, and that decision is made about a month before the workshop. No other scheduling decisions are made prior to the workshop. The afternoon activities are determined in the late morning or during lunch each day, and the speakers on the later days of the workshop are only decided one or two days in advance. Because of its fluid nature, each day's schedule is only announced on the previous afternoon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt a flexible, adaptive planning model: fix a few initial talks but leave most scheduling to evolve during the workshop; communicate daily schedules shortly in advance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Facility requirements to support collaborative work and virtual participation
rubrics_metrics.description: A large meeting room has tables, chairs, whiteboards, and a projection system. An adjacent lounge area has high-top tables, couches, and additional whiteboard space. There are five small breakout rooms with ample whiteboards, ceiling projectors, and meeting owls for virtual collaboration. Throughout, moveable partitions allow for flexible use and additional collaboration space.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure ample writable surfaces, projection, small breakout rooms, flexible partitions, and technology (meeting owls) to support hybrid/virtual collaboration and multiple concurrent activities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amenities, network access, and accessibility features
rubrics_metrics.description: A kitchen area is stocked with coffee, tea, and light refreshments throughout the day, and a social area with couches and games. The eduroam network is available along with AIM-provided wifi throughout the facility. There are four single-occupancy restrooms, including two all-gender restrooms and two with changing tables.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide refreshments, robust wifi (eduroam and local), comfortable social areas, and inclusive restroom/changing facilities to support participants' well-being and accessibility needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: AIM staff logistical and planning support for organizers
rubrics_metrics.description: The AIM staff works with the organizers on all aspects of the workshop planning and preparation. This includes the development of the participant list, preparation of lead-in material, and the planning the workshop activities. The administrative logistics, such as sending invitations, keeping track of who has accepted or declined, etc, is handled by the AIM staff.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rely on AIM staff to handle administrative tasks and to assist organizers (especially those with little prior experience of this fluid workshop style) both before and during the workshop.
